issues: At 1x the silhouette reads as a round fish with a pointed striped tail, not a squid with separate thrusting tentacles.
The long right-side appendage forms one rigid triangular mass; it does not suggest tentacles gathering and extending in pulses.
The face uses large rectangular eye sockets and broad interior bands, giving it a modern icon-like construction rather than an MM2/MM3 enemy face.
Black contour thickness is inconsistent around the lower body and tail joint, creating heavy black blocks instead of a controlled 1-pixel outline.
Several isolated blue and white steps along the tail produce a busy striped pattern that competes with the face.
The sprite appears to use black, white, cyan, medium blue, and dark blue within compact tile areas, exceeding the disciplined three-colour-plus-transparency look.
There is no visible mine or warning-state cue beyond the eyes; the current dark eyes do not establish a clear area for a red flash frame.
fixes: Replace the triangular tail with three or four individually separated 1-pixel-wide tentacle tips, leaving transparent gaps between them.
Orient the body vertically with a domed mantle above and short tentacles below or behind, so the squid silhouette reads at 1x.
Reduce the face to two compact eye clusters with one dark pupil pixel each; reserve those pupil pixels for red in the warning frame.
Use one dark outline colour, one main blue or cyan, and one light highlight colour per hardware sprite tile; remove one of the intermediate blues and most white striping.
Make the outer contour consistently one source pixel thick, especially beneath the body and where the tentacles attach.
Consolidate the interior shading into two or three larger clusters rather than horizontal bands and isolated stair-step pixels.
Create at least two animation frames: tentacles gathered close to the body, then tentacles extended backward for the thrust pulse.

issues: At 1x the silhouette reads as a fish, rocket, or single-eyed projectile rather than a floating robot squid.
The long pointed appendage on the right forms one striped wedge; it does not separate into readable tentacles or suggest a gather-and-thrust swimming motion.
The face is crowded: the two dark eye cavities merge with the heavy lower outline, weakening the flashing-eye concept.
Black clusters along the lower body and appendage joint are excessively thick and irregular compared with Capcom's controlled 1-pixel contouring.
The alternating cyan, blue, white, and purple bands in the right appendage create noisy striping rather than simple NES flat shading.
Several stair-steps around the dome, lower-left edge, and appendage tip lack a consistent pixel rhythm.
The sprite appears to exceed a practical single NES sprite palette in multiple 8x8 regions without a clear overlay-sprite rationale.
The asymmetrical side-mounted tentacle mass loses the compact, toy-like charm and clear anatomy typical of Mega Man 2-3 enemies.
fixes: Shorten the right appendage and divide its tip into three distinct 1-2-pixel tentacles with transparent gaps between them.
Give the body a compact dome or bell silhouette, then place the tentacles beneath or diagonally behind it so the squid anatomy reads at 1x.
Reduce the black underside to a controlled 1-pixel contour, reserving thicker black only for intentional shadow pockets.
Simplify each eye to a clean dark socket with a single cyan or white pupil; prepare an alternate frame replacing that light color with red for the warning flash.
Remove the horizontal striping and use one base blue plus one cyan highlight cluster on the body and tentacles.
Regularize curves with deliberate step patterns such as 1-1-2 or 1-2-2, especially on the dome and lower-left contour.
Limit each 8x8 region to black plus two blues, using a separate overlay sprite only if the red eye flash requires it.
Create at least two animation frames: tentacles compacted close to the body, then spread backward in a clear thrust pose.

issues: At 1x the silhouette reads more like a tiny fish or eyeball with a striped tail than a squid with gathering and thrusting tentacles.
The oversized circular head and two large square eye sockets use a modern mascot-like construction rather than the compact mechanical forms typical of Mega Man 2-3 enemies.
Detached or weakly connected black pixels above the rear edge and below the right appendage look like accidental fragments.
The lower outline is excessively heavy, forming a large black mass that obscures the body and tentacle separation.
The trailing appendages merge into one horizontally striped wedge instead of distinct tentacle clusters capable of showing a pulse animation.
The sprite uses too many blue and violet ramps within small tile areas; the layered band shading is not disciplined like an NES three-color sprite palette.
There is no visible red-eye warning state or mine-like mechanical detail to communicate its proximity trigger and explosive role.
fixes: Reduce the head to a simpler 12-14 px mechanical dome with a consistent one-pixel black contour.
Replace the striped rear wedge with three or four clearly separated tentacles, using one gathered frame and one splayed thrust frame.
Remove the detached black pixels above the rear and beneath the right side; connect necessary extremities with deliberate one-pixel joints.
Thin the bottom outline and carve background notches between tentacles so the silhouette remains readable at 1x.
Limit each 8x8 region to black plus two blues and one light cyan or white; remove the extra violet and intermediate blue bands.
Make the eyes smaller and more robotic, then reserve a red palette swap or red eye pixels for the warning frame.
Add one compact mine cue, such as a central seam, rivet, or small fuse-like sensor, without increasing the color count.

issues: The lower-left tentacle mass uses busy alternating blue and cyan stair-steps, becoming noisy at 1x instead of forming clean animated limbs.
The heavy black region between the dome and eyes muddies the face/body connection and makes the construction less readable.
The two eyes are oversized and unevenly integrated; the right eye projects as a box while the left eye is crowded by the central black column.
Several contour transitions are chunky or awkward, especially the upper-right dome, right eye edge, and hooked lower-right tentacle.
Black, white, blue, and cyan occur together in compact areas, making the palette usage harder to reconcile with a single NES sprite palette.
It reads as a cute squid, but mechanical mine cues are weak: there is no obvious casing seam, fuse/light, or distinct warning-eye treatment.
fixes: Reduce each eye by roughly one pixel in width and align both pupils and upper edges to create a cleaner Capcom-style face.
Remove one to two black pixels from the central face column so the eyes separate clearly from the body without a large dead black mass.
Simplify the lower-left area into two or three solid tentacle lobes; replace alternating cyan-blue steps with one contiguous shadow cluster and one highlight cluster.
Clean the dome into smoother 1-pixel stair-step runs, especially at the upper-right transition into the face.
Redraw the lower-right hook with a consistent one-pixel outline and a clearer gap between adjacent tentacles.
Reserve white primarily for the eyes and cyan for a single body highlight, keeping each 8x8 region closer to three opaque colors plus transparency.
Add a one- or two-pixel mechanical seam or warning lamp, and provide a separate alert frame that swaps the eye white or pupils to red before detonation.

issues: The silhouette reads more like a curled fish or seahorse than a floating squid; the lower blue mass forms one large hook instead of distinct gathered tentacles.

fixes: Replace the large lower curl with three short, separately readable tentacle tips, arranged in a compact gathered pose beneath the body.
Reduce each eye by roughly one pixel in width and height, round their outer corners, and separate them with a cleaner one-pixel black bridge.
Remove or shorten the right-side black bar so the outer contour ends immediately after the far eye.
Thin the heavy black regions around the center and lower-right edge to a consistent one-pixel outline wherever overlap is not required.
Reshape the top into a compact mechanical squid mantle with a more symmetrical dome and one small cyan highlight cluster.
Use black, one blue, and white as the primary sprite palette; reserve cyan or red for a layered highlight/eye-flash sprite.
Add a one- or two-pixel red eye state for the warning animation and create a second frame where the tentacles visibly spread backward for the thrust pulse.

Replace thick outline patches with deliberate 1-pixel contours, allowing thickness only where black also serves as interior separation.
Limit each local 8x8 region to black, blue, cyan or white plus transparency, avoiding unnecessary overlap of all four visible colors.

fixes: Compress the sprite to roughly 18x18 px and keep the main body around 12–14 px wide.
Replace the horizontal tail with three or four short tentacles beneath the body; make gathered and thrust animation frames by changing their spacing by 1–2 pixels.
Create two 2x2 eye clusters in the face, using one shared light color normally and red as a palette-swapped warning frame.
Round the upper mantle with deliberate 1-pixel steps and taper the lower body into the tentacle roots.
Remove the yellow strip or reserve it solely for the eyes; use black, white, and two blues in carefully separated sprite layers.

Add one small highlight cluster to the mantle and redistribute dark blue into compact shadow clusters instead of a large tail mass.

Keep each hardware-sprite region to black plus two main colors, using white as the face/highlight and one blue body tone; remove the isolated yellow unless it serves a clearly defined mechanical detail.

fixes: Compress the sprite to about 18x18 px: use an 11-12 px rounded mantle and keep all tentacles within another 5-7 px.

Use black, blue, and white for the normal frame; swap the eye pixels to red in a dedicated warning frame rather than carrying the large red stripe.

Partition the sprite so each 8x8 hardware piece uses no more than three visible colors plus transparency—for example black/blue/white for the mantle and black/white/red for the face.
Reduce the highlight to a small one- or two-pixel cluster that follows the mantle's curvature.
